topics.chapterTitle: Appendix A — A Modern C++ Diagnostic Desk Reference
topics.title: Start with the failed contract
topics.summary: A useful diagnosis begins with an observable discrepancy. “The application crashes” is a starting symptom. “The second render reads a title after its parsing buffer has been reused” identifies a lifetime hypothesis. “The destination changes after a rejected copy” identifies a state-guarantee discrepancy. “Two equal-priority records change order” identifies a presentation contract. State the discrepancy before changing implementation details.

blocks.text: Preserve the smallest reproducing input, the exact executable, compiler and library versions, build flags, arguments, working directory, exit status, and relevant output. Rebuilding the program before saving the failing binary can remove evidence. Reproducing with a new compiler can be useful, but it is a second experiment rather than a substitute for identifying what ran originally. The Linux book’s evidence-first habit applies directly to native application debugging.

blocks.text: Do not immediately replace a failing abstraction with a raw pointer or a hand-written loop. The defect may be a violated precondition, not a library limitation. Conversely, do not conceal a defect by adding a smart pointer around an object whose ownership is still ambiguous. Make one hypothesis-driven change and retain the case that demonstrated the original failure.

topics.chapterTitle: Appendix A — A Modern C++ Diagnostic Desk Reference
topics.title: Gate 1 — Translation and constraints
topics.summary: At translation time, inspect the first relevant diagnostic rather than the longest cascade. Confirm the selected language mode and that all required headers are included directly. A header that happens to arrive through another header on one implementation is not a dependable interface. When a concept fails, identify the expression or requirement that was not satisfied before weakening the constraint.

blocks.text: Separate “the requested syntax is unavailable” from “the requested operation violates the template’s domain.” A C++20 build should not be repaired by assuming a C++23 library helper exists. A checked integer function rejecting bool should not be repaired by removing its concept. One failure concerns environment capability; the other concerns an intentional API boundary.

blocks.text: Template diagnostics often become easier when reduced to a named type and one operation. Replace a long pipeline temporarily with local variables whose types can be inspected. Check the callable parameter and return types. A reference qualifier or an unexpected const element can explain a failure more directly than adding an unconstrained forwarding layer.

topics.title: Gate 2 — Linking and target composition
topics.summary: A declaration tells translation what an entity looks like. An out-of-line definition must also participate in the linked program when required. If the report’s implementation file is absent from the target, repeatedly including its header will not resolve the missing definition. Inspect the CMake target and the actual build command, not only the editor’s file tree.

blocks.text: Templates have additional visibility requirements because needed instantiations often require definitions to be available where used. Moving every template body to a source file without an explicit instantiation design can produce linking failures. Decide whether the template is header-defined or explicitly instantiated for a closed set of types. Both are designs; an accidental mixture is not.

blocks.text: Use separate build directories for different compilers and instrumentation modes. CMake caches toolchain decisions. A fresh directory makes it easier to establish what was configured than repeatedly editing a populated cache. Keep the source tree free of generated object files so a stale artifact cannot masquerade as a newly compiled result.

topics.chapterTitle: Appendix A — A Modern C++ Diagnostic Desk Reference
topics.title: Gate 3 — Ownership and lifetime
topics.summary: For each suspect object, ask who constructed it, who destroys it, who can replace its storage, and which aliases escaped. Trace raw pointers, references, iterators, spans, string views, lambda captures, and references embedded inside tuples. The absence of the * character does not imply the absence of a borrow.

blocks.text: A pointer can be non-null and still be unusable. An iterator can have a plausible address and still be invalidated. A shared pointer can retain a control block while exposing an aliased subobject under a separate lifetime relationship. A const reference can prevent mutation through one name while another alias changes the owner. Diagnose the entire relationship, not a single reassuring property.

blocks.text: The first safe repair is often to shorten the borrow’s scope or create an owning snapshot at a boundary. Retaining an ID and looking up the current object later can also be more appropriate than retaining a position. Do not use global storage merely to keep a local object alive; that changes lifetime, coupling, and concurrency assumptions throughout the program.

topics.chapterTitle: Appendix A — A Modern C++ Diagnostic Desk Reference
topics.title: Gate 4 — Invariants and failure guarantees
topics.summary: Write the invariant as a statement that can be evaluated before and after the operation. A buffer’s size must agree with its owned storage. A report’s accepted IDs must be unique. A quantity must stay within its domain. A moved-from custom owner may promise an empty state. These statements identify what a test should inspect beyond the immediate return value.

blocks.text: A basic exception guarantee preserves validity and avoids leaks under the operation’s contract. A strong guarantee preserves the specified observable state on failure. A nonthrowing operation promises that no exception escapes. These guarantees are not interchangeable, and each needs an explicit boundary. An operation can preserve a report while consuming input or changing a test fault counter.

blocks.text: Locate the commit point. If public state changes before the last potentially failing step, determine how rollback occurs or weaken the documented guarantee. Candidate construction followed by a suitable nonthrowing swap is a common solution for owning values, but allocator compatibility and member behavior still matter. Copy-and-swap is a technique, not a universal exemption from reviewing contracts.

topics.title: Gate 5 — Algorithms and representation
topics.summary: Write the input domain, range category, comparator requirements, destination extent, mutation effects, and result semantics. A lower bound is not a membership result. Stable sorting does not make output independent of input order. Reserved vector capacity does not create destination elements. A wider receiving variable does not widen an earlier narrow multiplication.

blocks.text: For a container change, include how positions are found and which references are retained. A list’s insertion cost near a known iterator does not include a search for that iterator. A hash table’s average lookup behavior does not supply deterministic traversal order. A view’s concise syntax does not supply independent element ownership or cached computation.

blocks.text: Use a hand-checkable reference case and a boundary case before adding a benchmark. Comparing two implementations that share the same faulty parser or comparator may confirm the same mistake twice. An independent oracle can be a manually computed result, a simpler algorithm over a bounded domain, or a reconstruction property whose assumptions are separately justified.

topics.chapterTitle: Appendix A — A Modern C++ Diagnostic Desk Reference
topics.title: Gate 6 — External completion and evidence
topics.summary: Distinguish successful computation from successful publication. A completed report string can exist while writing to its destination fails. A successful file close is not a universal crash-durability guarantee. A prior path inspection is not a held file handle. A nonzero application exit can be the correct result of an expected rejection test.

blocks.text: When reporting verification, name the actual configurations and cases executed. GCC and Clang may share the same standard library on a host. Sanitizers detect classes of defects in exercised executions; they do not prove semantic correctness or every path. Keep performance measurements separate from instrumented correctness runs, and do not publish a speedup without the baseline and workload that produced it.

topics.title: A reusable review record
topics.summary: Use one short record per investigated change: the requirement; the smallest failing case; the relevant owner and invariant; the proposed mechanism; the expected failure boundary; the observed result; and the remaining limitation. Preserve this record beside the regression fixture. It tells a future maintainer why the test exists and prevents a later “cleanup” from removing the condition that once exposed the defect.
